patient.chief_complaint: Right visual loss, right-sided weakness — progressive over 6 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. V is a 44-year-old paralegal with a history of three prior neurological admissions (all with negative workup attributed to FND) who presents with a 6-week history of progressive right visual loss and right-sided arm and leg weakness. She disputes the prior FND diagnoses, stating that a neurologist in another state 'found something' but is unable to provide records or specify what was found. She has migraine with aura but her prior auras have always been visual (zigzag fortification spectra) and brief (20-30 minutes). The current visual loss has been persistent for 6 weeks, which is completely atypical for migraine aura duration (aura should resolve within 60 minutes). She reports a large professional failure 6 weeks ago — a high-profile case she worked on concluded adversely — coinciding with symptom onset. She has a history of childhood sexual abuse. The diagnostic challenge here is: (1) she has risk factors for MS (female, prior demyelinating presentations possible but unconfirmed), (2) she has prior unconfirmed 'diagnosis by outside neurologist' that she cannot clarify, and (3) her prior FND attributions may have been premature, meaning organic disease cannot be excluded on the basis of prior FND labels alone. Every new presentation requires fresh evaluation.

additional_observations: SPECIFICALLY: No right occipital or posterior visual cortex lesion — visual homonymous hemianopia would require left occipital/visual cortex lesion
No optic nerve enhancement — no optic neuritis
mri.impression: Normal brain MRI. No occipital lesion, no optic nerve lesion, no demyelinating white matter disease. Complete right homonymous hemianopia has no structural correlate. Normal study. Clinical correlation recommended.

eeg.impression: Normal EEG. No posterior dominant rhythm asymmetry that would suggest occipital dysfunction. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.finding: Right eye VEP: P100 present at 102 ms (normal <115 ms). Normal amplitude 8.4 mcV (normal >4 mcV). NORMAL — visual pathway from right eye to occipital cortex is intact.
Left eye VEP: P100 present at 100 ms. Normal amplitude 9.1 mcV. NORMAL.

CRITICAL INTERPRETATION: VEPs are OBJECTIVE — they do not require patient cooperation. Normal P100 bilaterally with normal amplitude confirms intact visual pathway despite reported right homonymous hemianopia. Normal VEP with reported homonymous hemianopia = functional visual loss.

output.impression: Normal bilateral VEPs. Intact visual pathway confirmed objectively. The reported right homonymous hemianopia is NOT explained by any structural or electrophysiological visual pathway abnormality. Functional visual loss confirmed by VEP.
recommended_actions: Functional visual loss confirmed by VEP. FND diagnosis supported.

findings.finding: Goldman perimetry: Right visual field apparently absent to all targets. HOWEVER: fundoscopic examination NORMAL — no retinal disease, no optic disc pallor, no papilledema.
Spiral perimetry: Visual field expands in spiral fashion (getting larger) rather than remaining constant — classic sign of functional visual field loss

Confrontation test at varied distances: Visual field is the SAME SIZE regardless of how far patient stands from target — in organic homonymous hemianopia, the visual field size changes with distance (physiological optics). Same size at all distances = functional.

quantitative_data.VF_asymmetry: Apparent right field loss; no optic disc or retinal pathology

output.impression: Multiple positive signs of functional visual loss: spiral perimetry, non-physiological visual field size at varied distances, and normal fundoscopy with no retinal or optic nerve pathology. Combined with normal VEPs and normal MRI — functional visual loss confirmed.
recommended_actions: Functional visual loss confirmed by ophthalmology.

results.title: Prior FND diagnoses and re-evaluation: a systematic review

output.summary: Approximately 4% of FND diagnoses are later found to have underlying organic disease that was initially missed. However, in the context of positive functional signs, normal MRI, normal VEP, and normal CSF, the false-negative rate is very low. The correct approach is: (1) perform comprehensive current evaluation, (2) document positive FND signs, (3) obtain prior records for review, (4) not dismiss patient's concerns about prior misdiagnosis, (5) provide FND specialist referral with treatment plan rather than dismissal.

6-week persistent visual loss is >100x longer than maximum aura duration (60 min); migraine aura resolves completely; VEPs normal (post-migraine occipital spreading depression would normalize by now)

critical_actions: VEP is the definitive test for functional visual loss — objective, does not require cooperation
Obtain prior records to review prior 'diagnosis by outside neurologist'
Acknowledge patient's valid mistrust due to prior dismissal without treatment
contraindicated_actions: Dismissing as FND based on prior labels without fresh comprehensive evaluation — prior FND diagnoses do not prevent future organic disease
Assuming prior FND diagnoses were correct without reviewing documentation
key_reasoning_points: VISUAL EVOKED POTENTIALS are objective tests that do not require patient cooperation — normal P100 confirms intact visual pathway regardless of reported visual symptoms; this is the definitive test for functional visual loss

Spiral perimetry (visual field expanding in spiral pattern rather than remaining constant) and non-physiological visual field size at varying distances are positive FND signs specific to functional visual loss
Prior FND diagnoses should be reviewed, not automatically accepted — approximately 4% of FND diagnoses have organic disease initially missed; fresh evaluation is always required
Patient's mistrust of FND diagnosis is often justified when prior diagnoses were made without providing treatment — providing FND specialist treatment is both therapeutic and validates the diagnosis

red_herrings.intended_effect: Create uncertainty about FND diagnosis and prompt unnecessary additional testing
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal VEPs, normal MRI, normal CSF with normal oligoclonal bands, and positive functional signs (spiral perimetry, non-physiological VF) establish FND diagnosis; attempt to obtain prior records while proceeding with current evaluation
